sections.title: How does the One-time child costs calculator work?
sections.html:
The One-time child costs calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports transportation (In total) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (see the items' price range?); then you type in the basic bedding & blankets, the basic bedding & blankets (2x), the changing table and the baby monitor.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: The formula behind the One-time child costs calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Transportation=(infant car seats, stroller, sling ÷ wrap carrier, diaper bag)
Nursery=(crib ÷ Bassinet, changing table, co-sleeper, basic bedding & blankets, baby monitor)
Feeding=(bottles ÷ nipples, bib, bottle brush, electric ÷ manual breast pump, nursing bras, nursing pillow, storage bag, are you planning to express?)
Bath=(baby towel with hood, infant bathtub, brush & comb, baby nail clippers, washcloths)
Other=(pacifier, anything else?)
Transportation=(infant car seat (2x), double stroller, sling ÷ wrap carrier (2x), diaper bag)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The One-time child costs calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the basic bedding & blankets — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the One-time child costs calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns transportation (In total), derived from the basic bedding & blankets. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the One-time child costs calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the basic bedding & blankets, which is 37 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter crib/Bassinet in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Crib/Bassinet opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the One-time child costs calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
